title: CITES, CMS and Other Wildlife Conventions

cards.b:
Prelims often asks which treaty does what: trade, migratory species, wetlands or whaling. Many questions give a species and ask which Appendix or convention applies.

A clean table in your head removes most confusion.

Keep a three-line table: CITES for trade, CMS for migration, Ramsar for wetlands. Most wrong options swap these.

The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora was signed at Washington in 1973 and came into force in 1975. India joined in 1976. The secretariat is in Geneva, hosted by UNEP. CITES works through permits, not outright bans on all trade.

  • Appendix I: threatened with extinction; trade almost banned (tiger, rhino, Asian elephant).
  • Appendix II: trade regulated; may become threatened.
  • Appendix III: a country asks others to help control trade in a species.

The Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals, also the Bonn Convention, was adopted in 1979 (in force 1983). India is a party. It has Appendix I (endangered migratory species with strict protection) and Appendix II (species needing international cooperation).

Agreements under CMS: the Siberian Crane MoU (1998, India signed), the Dugong MoU, the Raptors MoU and the Marine Turtles MoU. India hosted CMS COP13 at Gandhinagar in February 2020, with the great Indian bustard as its mascot.

• Ramsar (1971): wetlands of international importance.
  • World Heritage (1972): natural and cultural sites.
  • IWC (1946): whaling; moratorium on commercial whaling from 1986. India is a member and is against whaling.
  • UNCLOS (1982): the law of the sea.
  • Bern, Lusaka and Lusaka Agreement: regional.
  • Convention on Wetlands, CMS, CITES and World Heritage together make the "biodiversity cluster".

CITES is applied in India through the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, and through the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act and Customs rules. The 2022 amendment to the WPA gave legal basis for CITES permits and a Management Authority. The Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (2007) tracks trade in tiger bone, rhino horn, pangolin scales and star tortoises.

India has proposed or supported moves to keep some species, such as the Indian star tortoise, at Appendix I.

Appendix I: tiger, leopards, snow leopard, Asian elephant, Indian rhino, red panda. Appendix II: most orchids, some sharks. The Indian star tortoise was moved to Appendix I in 2019. Pangolin species were moved to Appendix I in 2016. Ivory trade bans date from 1989.

Movements between appendices are decided at the CITES COP, held every three years.

Some say legal markets (for example, in ivory) fund conservation. Others say they cover illegal trade. India opposes legal trade in ivory. Community-based harvest, such as for vicuna wool, is cited as proof that regulated trade can help.

CITES has weak punishment for violators and is not designed to protect habitats.

India lies on the Central Asian Flyway, used by birds such as the bar-headed goose and Amur falcon. The Amur falcon at Doyang reservoir (Nagaland) is a conservation story: hunting was banned and now the village is a tourism site. Chilika, Keoladeo and Pong Dam host migratory birds.

• CITES: 1973 signed, 1975 in force. India 1976.
  • CMS: 1979. India hosted COP13, 2020.
  • Ramsar: 1971.
  • World Heritage: 1972.
  • IWC: 1946; moratorium 1986.

CITES COPs meet roughly every three years; the CMS COP meets every three years too, and its Scientific Council advises it. A Prelims favourite is the Appendix system, so memorise what I, II and III mean.

Prelims-style: "Which convention regulates international trade in endangered species?" (CITES). "Which treaty protects migratory animals across borders?" (CMS).

Mains-style: "Examine how international conventions help India protect wildlife." Structure: CITES and CMS role; Ramsar and WHC; WPA link; wildlife crime; limits; way forward.

Use one Indian example per convention: tiger bone under CITES, Amur falcon under CMS, Chilika under Ramsar.
